body.v2n1-01-transit-housing-prices.intr: The relationship between transport accessibility and property values is one of the fundamental themes of urban economics. The classic monocentric city model predicts that a reduction in transport costs raises the value of plots located far from the centre. Empirical studies conducted in various countries generally confirm this, but estimates of the effect vary considerably.

The opening of a new light rail line in the agglomeration under study in 2022 created a natural experiment. The aim of the study is to estimate the resulting change in housing prices, trace its dynamics over time and space, and relate it to the change in job accessibility.
body.v2n1-01-transit-housing-prices.meth: The source data comprise 18 thousand registered transactions and 28 thousand listings of flats for sale for 2018–2024. For listings, the last asking prices before removal from publication were used. All properties were geocoded and supplemented with characteristics: floor area, floor, year of construction and building material, and distance to the centre, parks and schools.

Job accessibility was calculated from public transport timetables and data on the location of employment. The hedonic model for the logarithm of the price per square metre includes property characteristics, district and quarter-period fixed effects, and the interaction of the impact zone indicator (up to 800 m from a station) with the “announcement”, “construction” and “operation” periods.
body.v2n1-01-transit-housing-prices.resu: The dynamics of the price difference between the impact zone and the control zone are shown in Fig. 1. Before the construction announcement, the differences are statistically insignificant, which supports the parallel trends assumption. After the announcement in 2019, the difference begins to grow and reaches 6.8% in the operation period.

Estimates of the main model and its modifications are given in Table 1. The effect for peripheral districts is almost three times larger than for the middle zone, while in the centre it does not differ statistically from zero.
body.v2n1-01-transit-housing-prices.figu: Fig. 1. Difference in price per square metre between the impact zone and the control zone by year, %
body.v2n1-01-transit-housing-prices.tabl: Table 1. Estimates of the hedonic difference-in-differences model (dependent variable: log price per m²)
body.v2n1-01-transit-housing-prices.disc: The magnitude of the effect lies in the middle of the range typical of international studies of rapid rail transit. The rise in prices even before the line opened indicates that the market capitalises expectations, which is important for the timing of land value capture mechanisms.

The heterogeneity of the effect across zones is consistent with theory: where accessibility was already high, the new line adds little. A limitation of the study is the use of asking prices for part of the sample; however, the estimate based on transactions only is close to the main one.
body.v2n1-01-transit-housing-prices.conc: The opening of the light rail line raised housing prices in the impact zone by 6.8%, with the largest effect observed on the periphery. This provides a rationale for using instruments that capture part of the value uplift to finance transport projects.
The concept of the circular economy implies abandoning the linear “take–make–dispose” model in favour of closed loops in which products and materials retain their value for as long as possible. A considerable part of research and policy programmes is oriented towards large companies that have the resources to restructure their production processes.

Small and medium-sized enterprises face different constraints: they have less capital, fewer competencies and less bargaining power in supply chains. At the same time, they are more flexible and closer to local communities. The aim of this review is to systematise empirical evidence on the factors that hinder and facilitate the adoption of circular practices in small and medium-sized businesses.
body.v2n1-03-circular-economy-sme.method: The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Bibliographic databases were searched using combinations of the terms “circular economy”, “small and medium-sized business” and their Russian-language equivalents. Empirical studies (surveys, case studies, interviews, econometric studies) published in 2015–2025 in English or Russian were included.

Of the 1,146 records retrieved, 214 studies underwent full-text assessment after removal of duplicates and screening of abstracts, and 72 met the inclusion criteria. Barriers and drivers were coded independently by two researchers according to a pre-developed scheme; inter-coder agreement was κ = 0.79.
body.v2n1-03-circular-economy-sme.result: The included studies cover 28 countries, but 61% of them are based on data from Western European countries. There are only five studies on the countries of Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The frequency with which the main barriers are mentioned is presented in Fig. 1.

The drivers of the adoption of circular practices are grouped in Table 1. Economic motives — reducing the costs of raw materials and waste disposal — are mentioned most often, but in studies of family businesses the owners’ values play a substantial role.
body.v2n1-03-circular-economy-sme.figure: Fig. 1. Frequency of mention of barriers in the included studies, % (n = 72)
Table 1. Main drivers of the adoption of circular practices
Savings on raw materials and disposal
body.v2n1-03-circular-economy-sme.discus: The dominance of financial barriers and drivers shows that for small businesses circularity is primarily a matter of economics rather than of the environmental agenda. Support measures that reduce initial costs and risks are therefore in greatest demand. At the same time, subsidies without advisory support often fail to bring about lasting change.

The geographical bias of the evidence base limits the transferability of the conclusions: the institutional environment, access to finance and recycling infrastructure differ substantially across countries. Filling this gap is an important task for regional research.
body.v2n1-03-circular-economy-sme.conclu: The adoption of circular practices in small and medium-sized businesses is determined primarily by economic incentives and supply chain requirements. Effective policy should combine financial support with the development of competencies and infrastructure.
body.v2n1-04-urban-soil-microbiome.intro: Soil microorganisms govern the cycling of carbon and nitrogen, soil structure and plant health. In cities, soils are subject to strong anthropogenic pressure — compaction, contamination, the introduction of fill materials — yet parks, especially old ones, can serve as reservoirs of microbial diversity.
The aim of this communication is to present the first data on the composition and diversity of bacterial communities in urban park soils and to identify the main factors determining their structure.
body.v2n1-04-urban-soil-microbiome.metho: In six parks (P1–P6) aged from 15 to 120 years, four composite samples were collected from the 0–10 cm layer in each of three site types (lawn, woody vegetation, path verge). DNA was extracted using a commercial kit, and the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified and sequenced. The sequences were processed to resolve amplicon sequence variants; diversity was assessed using the Shannon index, and differences in community structure by PERMANOVA on a Bray–Curtis distance matrix.
body.v2n1-04-urban-soil-microbiome.resul: The Shannon index differed between site types (Fig. 1): the highest values were recorded under woody vegetation and the lowest along paths, where soil bulk density reached 1.55 g/cm³. The results of the PERMANOVA are given in Table 1.
body.v2n1-04-urban-soil-microbiome.figur: Fig. 1. Shannon index of bacterial communities by site type in young and old parks
body.v2n1-04-urban-soil-microbiome.table: Table 1. Factors in the structure of bacterial communities (PERMANOVA, 999 permutations)
body.v2n1-04-urban-soil-microbiome.discu: The strong influence of site type and soil bulk density points to recreational compaction as the leading factor in the impoverishment of microbial communities. This is consistent with data for natural recreational areas. The weak influence of heavy metals may be explained by their moderate concentrations in the parks studied. The practical conclusion is that a well-organised network of paths and the protection of tree root zones from trampling help to preserve soil biodiversity.
body.v2n1-04-urban-soil-microbiome.concl: The bacterial diversity of urban park soils is determined primarily by site type, pH and soil compaction. Old parks with preserved tree stands are important reservoirs of soil microbial diversity.
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.intro.0: The output of wind farms is determined by wind speed, which changes rapidly and is poorly predictable. Forecast errors make it necessary to hold capacity in reserve and incur balancing costs, so improving forecast accuracy has a direct economic effect.
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.intro.1: Numerical weather prediction forecasts are the main source of information about future wind, but their spatial resolution is insufficient to account for local conditions. The aim of the study is to develop a model that extracts additional information from weather forecasts by means of feature engineering and gradient boosting.
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.methods.0: Hourly output data from the 40 wind turbines of an anonymised 120 MW farm for January 2021 to June 2025 were used, together with an archive of numerical weather prediction forecasts with lead times of up to 48 hours for nine grid nodes. A total of 86 features were constructed, including wind speed at heights of 10, 100 and 150 m, wind shear, the spatial wind speed gradient and an atmospheric stability indicator.
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.methods.1: The gradient boosting model was trained separately for each group of forecast horizons. Data for 2021–2023 were used for training, 2024 for hyperparameter tuning and 2025 for the final evaluation. Performance was measured by the normalised root-mean-square error (NRMSE) relative to installed capacity.
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.results.0: The dependence of the error on the forecast horizon for the models compared is shown in Fig. 1. At horizons of up to three hours, the persistence method is competitive, but from six hours onwards the models based on weather forecasts substantially outperform it.
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.results.1: Summary results for the 24-hour horizon are given in Table 1. The proposed model outperforms all alternatives, and during the passage of weather fronts its advantage over the power-curve model reaches 4.5 percentage points.
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.figure.capt: Fig. 1. Normalised root-mean-square forecast error as a function of horizon, %
body.sub-wind-power-forecast.table.capti: Table 1. Forecast performance at the 24-hour horizon (2025 test period)
The advantage of the proposed model is explained primarily by the use of spatial features: the wind speed gradient between grid nodes makes it possible to “see” an approaching front earlier. The recurrent network achieves similar performance but requires an order of magnitude more computational resources and is harder to interpret.
A limitation of the study is the use of data from a single farm; the transferability of the features to farms in other climatic conditions requires verification.
Gradient boosting with features extracted from numerical weather prediction forecasts provides accurate and computationally efficient short-term wind power forecasting suitable for practical application.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.intro.0: Natural fibres — flax, hemp and jute — have low density, adequate specific strength and a renewable raw material base. In combination with biodegradable polymers such as polylactic acid, they make it possible to obtain fully bio-based composites.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.intro.1: The main problem with such materials is the hydrophilicity of the fibre, which impairs adhesion to the hydrophobic matrix and leads to water absorption and degradation in service. The aim of the study is to compare the effectiveness of alkali and silane fibre treatments in improving the resistance of the composites to weathering.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.methods.0: Short flax fibre 3–5 mm long was used. Alkali treatment was carried out with a 5% sodium hydroxide solution for 1 h; silane treatment with a 2% aminosilane solution in a water–ethanol mixture. Composites with a fibre mass fraction of 30% were produced by hot pressing at 185 °C.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.methods.1: Accelerated ageing was carried out in a chamber with 12-h cycles: 8 h of ultraviolet irradiation at 60 °C and 4 h of moisture condensation at 50 °C. Tensile and flexural tests were performed after 0, 500 and 1000 h; at least seven specimens were tested for each condition.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.results.0: The change in tensile strength during ageing is shown in Fig. 1. Initially, the composites with alkali-treated fibre had the highest strength, but after 1000 h their advantage disappeared.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.results.1: Summary mechanical properties and water absorption are given in Table 1. Silane treatment reduced water absorption almost by half and ensured the best retention of properties.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.figure.capti: Fig. 1. Tensile strength of the composites as a function of ageing duration, MPa
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.table.captio: Table 1. Properties of the composites before and after 1000 h of ageing
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.discussion.0: The increase in initial strength after alkali treatment is associated with the removal of hemicelluloses and increased fibre surface roughness, but the hydrophilicity of the fibre is retained. Silane treatment forms a hydrophobic layer on the fibre surface that is chemically bonded to the matrix, which explains the better retention of properties during ageing.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.discussion.1: Electron microscopy of the fracture surfaces confirms this: in the untreated composites, fibre pull-out from the matrix is observed after ageing, whereas in the silanised specimens fracture occurs predominantly through the fibres.
body.sub-flax-biocomposites.conclusion.0: Silane treatment of flax fibre substantially improves the resistance of polylactic acid-based biocomposites to weathering and can be recommended for outdoor products.
